1.note: The implied “you” in the verb **Hear** is plural here because Elisha is addressing everyone who is present. This included elders of Samaria, the king, and some officers he brought with him, as the next verse indicates. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [a message from Yahweh]

1.q: כֹּ֣ה ׀ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה כָּ⁠עֵ֤ת ׀ מָחָר֙ סְאָֽה־סֹ֣לֶת בְּ⁠שֶׁ֗קֶל וְ⁠סָאתַ֧יִם שְׂעֹרִ֛ים בְּ⁠שֶׁ֖קֶל בְּ⁠שַׁ֥עַר שֹׁמְרֽוֹן
1.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that at this time tomorrow, a seah of flour will be at a shekel and two seahs of barley will be at a shekel in the gate of Samaria]

A **seah** was a dry measure equivalent to 7.7 liters or about six quarts. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this in terms of modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote.
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:25. Alternate translation: [will sell for a silver shekel … will sell for a silver shekel]

2.note: The author is using one thing that this **captain** did for the **king**, supporting him with his **hand**, to mean everything that he did as the king’s personal attendant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who was the king’s personal attendant]

2.q: הִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה עֹשֶׂ֤ה אֲרֻבּוֹת֙ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם הֲ⁠יִהְיֶ֖ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
2.note: The captain is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Even if Yahweh were to make windows in the heavens, this thing could not be!]

2.q: הִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה עֹשֶׂ֤ה אֲרֻבּוֹת֙ בַּ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם הֲ⁠יִהְיֶ֖ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
2.note: The captain is using a common expression of his culture, saying **Behold**, naming a person, and then using a participle to describe an action, to indicates that a person is about to do that action. The captain may be speaking either conditionally or sarcastically. Alternate translation: [Even if Yahweh is about to make windows in the heavens, this thing could not be!] or [I suppose Yahweh is about to make windows in the heavens. Even so, this thing could not be!]
Elisha is responding to the captain by using the same common expression. Alternate translation: [You are about to see this with your eyes]

It might seem that the expression **seeing with your eyes** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could say this in a way that would be natural. Alternate translation: [You are about to witness this personally]

3.q: וְ⁠אַרְבָּעָ֧ה אֲנָשִׁ֛ים הָי֥וּ מְצֹרָעִ֖ים פֶּ֣תַח הַ⁠שָּׁ֑עַר
3.note: The author is introducing these **lepers** as new participants in the story. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation.
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [to each other]

The lepers are using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We should not just sit here until we die!]

4.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [If we say that we will enter the city] or [If we decide to enter the city]
See how you translated the same expression in 3:23.

The lepers are using **let us fall** as a common expression of their culture to mean “let us desert.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 29:3. Alternate translation: [and let us desert]

5.note: To translate the term **arose** here and in verse 7, how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [So they took action]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.

6.note: Here, **the camp of Aram** represents the Aramean soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the Aramean soldiers]

The author is not referring to a specific **horse**. He means the horses of the Aramean army in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [horses]

The author is using **his brother** as a common expression of his culture to mean “his fellow soldier.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his fellow soldier]
It might seem that saying **against us** twice would be to express extra information that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can omit the first instance of this phrase.

The author is using **the kings of the Hittites and the kings of the Egyptians** to represent these kings and their armies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the armies of the kings of the Hittites and the kings of the Egyptians]

At this time, all of Egypt was ruled by one king. This expression is probably plural because it is in parallel with the expression **the kings of the Hittites**. It may be more natural in your language to use a singular expression. Alternate translation: [and the king of Egypt]

7.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [leaving the camp just as it was]

While the word **life** is singular in form, it refers to the lives of all of the Aramean soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “life.” Alternate translation: [for their lives] or [to save their lives]

8.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they carried away valuable possessions]

9.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 7:3. Alternate translation: [to each other]

The lepers are speaking of **punishment** as if it were a living thing that could **find** them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people will punish us]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point such as the implications of what they had just been saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated this expression in 3:23.

The speakers are not telling their fellow lepers to **go** somewhere. They are encouraging them to do what they are suggesting. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Let us go ahead and come]
In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [and let us go]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters may use the term “house” to mean all the people who live in the same house as a person, including family members and servants. Alternate translation: [the household of the king]

10.note: The author is not referring to a specific **gatekeeper**. As the pronoun **them** later in this verse and the plural form in the next verse indicate, there were several gatekeepers on duty. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the gatekeepers of the city]

The lepers are not referring to a specific **horse** or **donkey**. They mean the Arameans’ horses and donkeys in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but the horses were tied, and the donkeys were tied]

In both instances, the expression **was tied** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but their horses and donkeys were still at their tethers]

11.note: Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and some people informed the house of the king] or [and house of the king was informed]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [within the city]

12.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר כִּֽי־יֵצְא֤וּ מִן־הָ⁠עִיר֙ וְ⁠נִתְפְּשֵׂ֣⁠ם חַיִּ֔ים וְ⁠אֶל־הָ⁠עִ֖יר נָבֹֽא
12.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [telling themselves that we will come out from the city, and they will capture us alive, and they will enter into the city]
Here the word **For** introduces the expected result of an action. Use a connecting word or phrase that will indicate this in your language. Alternate translation: [Because we have done this,]

13.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [the horses that remain in the city]

13.q: הִנָּ֗⁠ם כְּ⁠כָל־ה⁠המון יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁאֲרוּ־בָ֔⁠הּ הִנָּ֕⁠ם כְּ⁠כָל־הֲמ֥וֹן יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁר־תָּ֑מּוּ
13.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second phrase makes the meaning of the first more specific by indicating that those who **remain** in the city **have finished**, that is, they are on the verge of death. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Behold them, like all of the multitude of Israel who remain in it, who are about to die]

Here, **Israel** represents “Israelites,” specifically those in the city of Samaria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the many Israelites]

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:6. Alternate translation: [the Aramean soldiers]

16.note: See how you decided to represent the quantity of a seah in [7:1](ta:07).
See how you translated the similar expressions in [7:1](ta:07). Alternate translation: [sold for a silver shekel … sold for a silver shekel]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 6:33. Alternate translation: [who was his personal attendant]

The author is using **over the gate** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in charge of the gate” or “responsible for supervising the gate.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to be responsible for the gate]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:33. Alternate translation: [when the king came to him]

18.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֗י כְּ⁠דַבֵּר֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר סָאתַ֨יִם שְׂעֹרִ֜ים בְּ⁠שֶׁ֗קֶל וּֽ⁠סְאָה־סֹ֨לֶת֙ בְּ⁠שֶׁ֔קֶל יִהְיֶה֙ כָּ⁠עֵ֣ת מָחָ֔ר בְּ⁠שַׁ֖עַר שֹׁמְרֽוֹן
18.note: Here and in the next two verses, the author is repeating details from [7:1–2](ta:07) and 7:17. He is using this repetition to signal the end of his account of how the famine in Samaria ended. Use a natural form in your language for concluding an account with a repetition of some of its details. See how you translated the quotations from Elisha and the captain in [7:1–2](ta:07), and translate them the same way here and in the next verse so that the repetition will be evident to your readers.
